questions.title: Sodium channel inactivation underlies the absolute refractory period
questions.subject: neuro
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Nerve and Muscle Physiology > Action Potential
questions.question: The absolute refractory period of an action potential occurs primarily because of which specific ion channel mechanism?

options.C: Sodium channels are only partially active
options.D: Potassium channels are completely, partially active

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is sodium channels, not potassium channels, whose inactivated state underlies the absolute refractory period; potassium channels are, if anything, still open and contributing to repolarization at this time.
explanations.B: Correct. During and immediately after depolarization, the great majority of voltage-gated sodium channels sit in the inactivated state, in which their inactivation gate blocks the pore regardless of voltage, so no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential until enough channels have returned to the closed, activatable state. Only once enough sodium channels have returned from inactivated to the closed, resting state does excitability begin to recover.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Describing sodium channels as merely 'partially active' understates the mechanism; during the absolute refractory period they are specifically inactivated (unavailable), not simply reduced in activity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Potassium channel state is not what defines the absolute refractory period; the defining, rate-limiting event is sodium channel inactivation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the absolute refractory period is caused by voltage-gated sodium channels sitting in the inactivated state, making them unavailable to reopen regardless of stimulus strength.
